exam: A 13‑year‑old girl presents with a 9 cm/yr height increase and menarche 6 months ago; hemoglobin is 10 g/dL. What investigations do you order and why? — Serial height, WHO chart, Tanner stage, CBC and ferritin to assess growth adequacy and iron status.

A 15‑year‑old boy reports knee pain for 3 months, worse at night, with a palpable distal femoral mass. What is your next step? — Urgent imaging (X‑ray/MRI) to rule out osteosarcoma; do not attribute to growth‑related pain.
How does hypothyroidism alter adolescent growth, and what laboratory test confirms it? — It slows linear growth and delays bone age; elevated TSH with low free T4 confirms diagnosis.

In a low‑resource clinic without bone‑age X‑ray, how can you differentiate constitutional delay from pathological short stature? — Use growth velocity, parental heights, and Tanner stage; constitutional delay shows delayed puberty with normal velocity.

A girl with sickle cell disease has stalled growth and Hb 7 g/dL. What management priorities apply? — Treat anemia (transfusion or iron if deficient), optimise nutrition, and ensure disease‑modifying therapy (hydroxyurea) to improve growth.
Why is high‑dose glucocorticoid therapy avoided in a child with growth failure? — Glucocorticoids suppress growth‑hormone axis and cause bone loss, worsening growth delay.

What red‑flag symptom in an adolescent with rapid weight loss warrants urgent referral? — Unexplained weight loss > 10 % of body weight with loss of height velocity suggests malignancy or chronic disease.

Explain how you would counsel a family about normal adolescent growth versus when to seek medical review. — Emphasise expected height velocity ranges, importance of nutrition, and that persistent pain, slowed growth, or anemia require evaluation.
ai.title: Adolescent Growth and Puberty
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Adolescent growth is a rapid increase in height, weight and bone length driven by hormonal changes of puberty. Recognising normal patterns and red‑flags helps detect growth disorders, anemia, and early malignancy in low‑resource settings.

b: Height velocity > 8 cm/yr in girls or > 10 cm/yr in boys suggests a spurt
Bone age within 1 year of chronological age is normal
sections.p: A growth spurt is a period of accelerated linear growth lasting 6–24 months, usually occurring between ages 10–14 in girls and 12–16 in boys. Diagnosis relies on serial height measurements plotted on WHO growth charts and assessment of Tanner stage.

b: Mild: velocity 1–2 cm/yr below expected, final height ≥ 3rd percentile
Moderate: velocity 2–4 cm/yr below, final height 3rd–10th percentile
Severe: velocity > 4 cm/yr below, final height < 3rd percentile
sections.p: Growth disorders are staged by deviation from expected velocity and final height percentile.

b: Physiologic: normal puberty, adequate nutrition
Endocrine: hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency, Cushing syndrome
Chronic disease: HIV, TB, sickle cell disease, severe malaria
Nutritional: iron‑deficiency anemia, protein‑energy malnutrition
Genetic/structural: Turner syndrome, skeletal dysplasia, osteosarcoma
sections.p: Most adolescents have physiologic growth, but failure to thrive signals pathology.

b: Rapid increase in height and shoe size
Weight gain lagging behind height
Mild knee or shin pain during growth (physiologic) versus persistent localized pain (red flag)
Fatigue, pallor → consider anemia
sections.p: Students should ask about recent height change, menarche, weight gain, fatigue, and bone pain.

t.b: Is growth velocity appropriate for age and sex? → confirms normal spurt or flags abnormal pattern
Where does the child fall compared with peers? → identifies under‑ or over‑growth
What stage of sexual maturation? → correlates hormonal drive with growth
Is anemia present? → iron‑deficiency common in girls with menarche
Is iron store depleted? → < 15 µg/L confirms iron‑deficiency
Is hypothyroidism contributing? → elevated TSH, low free T4
Is skeletal maturation delayed or advanced? → helps differentiate endocrine vs constitutional delay

b: Persistent localized bone pain, swelling or night pain → possible osteosarcoma
Height velocity falling > 2 cm/yr below expected for > 6 months
Severe anemia (Hb < 8 g/dL) with tachycardia or syncope
Signs of endocrine crisis (e.g., severe hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency)
sections.p: Identify signs that require urgent referral.

b: Physiologic spurt: reassurance, nutrition counselling, iron supplementation if ferritin low
Hypothyroidism: levothyroxine (replace deficient hormone) – avoid high‑dose steroids
Growth hormone deficiency: recombinant GH (if available) – avoid glucocorticoids which blunt growth
Chronic disease (HIV, TB, sickle cell): disease‑specific therapy, ensure adequate calories and micronutrients
Osteosarcoma suspicion: urgent referral for imaging and oncology
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, optimise nutrition and monitor growth.

b: Measure height every 3 months until growth plate closure
Repeat ferritin and CBC in girls after menarche
Vaccinate against hepatitis B and provide deworming to reduce chronic inflammation
Educate families on balanced diet rich in iron, protein and calcium
Constitutional growth delay – slower velocity but normal final height
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis – joint pain vs physiologic knee pain
Nutritional rickets – bone pain and growth faltering but with bowed legs and low calcium
sections.p: Conditions that mimic normal growth spurt or cause similar complaints.

b: Normal hemoglobin may mask iron deficiency if ferritin not measured (acute phase reaction raises ferritin)
Bone age may appear normal in early osteosarcoma; rely on clinical pain pattern
TSH can be falsely normal in central hypothyroidism – check free T4

whenToSeekHelp: Severe localized bone pain or swelling
